news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire schools face first-time £23m deficit as specialist support demand rises
news_drafts.lead: Lincolnshire County Council's schools budget ran £23 million over in 2025/26, marking the first time the dedicated schools grant—the government funding for schools—has moved into deficit. The shortfall was driven principally by the high needs block, which pays for specialist educational support and services. Demand for these services has continued to rise, creating structural pressure the council says its reviews have not yet resolved. The council's earmarked reserves—money it has set aside for specific purposes—also fell £8.3 million short of forecast to £125.1 million. The council's auditors concluded, however, that strong overall reserve balances mean no significant financial sustainability risk.
news_drafts.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire faces £25m schools deficit dependent on government funding approval
news_drafts.lead: Lincolnshire's spending on schools overspent by £13.4m in 2025-26, revealing a structural deficit of £25m once school reserves are excluded. The dedicated schools grant (DSG), which funds schools, was strained by continued pressure in the high needs block (support for children with special educational needs and disabilities). The council states that government will support approximately 90 per cent of the deficit through 31 March 2026, but only if the council submits an approved special educational needs and disabilities reform plan. The council also wrote off £5.3m in carry-forward overspends from day-to-day services—including £5m in children's social care and adult care combined—rather than roll them into next year's budget, to avoid compounding existing demand pressures already forecast for 2026-27.

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire overspent day-to-day budget by £7.4m (1.1%) in year to March 2026, with Children's Social Care at nearly £5m and Adult Frailty at £4.3m
news_drafts.lead: Lincolnshire County Council overran its day-to-day spending budget by £7.4m (1.1% of the total) in the year to March 2026, driven by surging costs in social care and other demand-led services. Rather than carrying forward these overspends, the council is writing them off, effectively accepting that these demand-led pressures are structural. Children's Social Care alone overran by nearly £5m, and Adult Frailty by about £4.3m. The council's medium-term financial plan, approved in February, already flagged limited headroom beyond 2026-27 and is now under review. The council has also explicitly earmarked its £46.9m Financial Volatility Reserve for costs of any future restructuring of council boundaries, signalling structural uncertainty about its future.

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: Government imposed two-unitary LGR against council's single-unitary preference
findings.detail: The council submitted a Local Government Reorganisation proposal in November 2025 advocating for a single unitary authority for Lincolnshire. The government decided instead to reorganise the area into two unitary authorities. This overruling of the council's preference introduces uncertainty about future governance arrangements, service delivery models and transition costs.
findings.matters: LGR is a structural change affecting finances, governance and service continuity; councils' preferences being overridden creates execution risk and potential unexpected costs during transition that a lender must account for.
findings.figures: Decision imposed rather than negotiated; no quantified impact described
findings.quote: Although the Council's proposal advocated for a single unitary authority, the Government ultimately decided that Lincolnshire would be reorganised into two unitary authorities covering the area previously administered by Lincolnshire County Council.

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves fell £8.3m short of forecast
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves dropped from £159.3m to £125.1m, representing an adverse variance of £8.3m against the forecasted balance of £133.4m. This faster-than-planned drawdown occurred alongside the DSG moving to deficit and the General Fund remaining static at £24.2m. Despite this variance, KPMG concluded the council's strong reserve balances meant no significant financial sustainability risk.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns faster than forecast suggest either optimistic budgeting or emerging pressures; a lender tracks whether councils are consuming buffers faster than expected, which can signal medium-term stress.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £125.1m actual vs £133.4m forecast; adverse variance £8.3m; General Fund £24.2m unchanged; DSG reserve negative
findings.quote: however the reported position of £125.1m represented an adverse variance of £8.3m from the forecast reserves balance of £133.4m

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspent £23m, moved to negative reserve for first time
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £23.0 million in 2025/26, driven primarily by the High Needs Block as demand for specialist educational support and services continued to rise. 2025/26 was the first year the DSG reserve moved into negative position. The council has established arrangements to review High Needs effectiveness but the deficit persists as structural demand pressure.
findings.matters: A £23m structural overspend in a ring-fenced grant that now carries an accumulated deficit indicates sustained demand pressures the council cannot control; this creates an unfunded liability that could eventually require general fund support.
findings.figures: £23.0 million DSG overspend; High Needs Block as principal driver; first year in negative DSG reserve
findings.quote: In addition, the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) recorded an overspend of £23.0 million. This was principally attributable to the High Needs Block, reflecting a continued increase in the number of children and young people requiring specialist educational support and services.

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: CQC rated adult social care 'Requires Improvement'; identified as significant VFM weakness
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission assessed the Council's adult social care as 'Requires Improvement' due to governance and risk management weaknesses. The CQC found that governance structures existed but were not demonstrably effective, with risk registers not consistently linked to outcomes and governance reporting failing to show how audit findings and stakeholder feedback drove service improvements. KPMG identified this as a significant risk to the Council's ability to achieve economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.matters: A major service failing to demonstrate effective governance and outcomes for vulnerable residents signals management control weaknesses; a lender needs confidence that leadership can correct substantive operational failures.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; flagged as significant VFM risk requiring follow-up audit procedures
findings.quote: Due to the findings identified by the CQC regarding the Council's adult service provision we have identified a significant risk regarding the arrangements of this service.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan has limited headroom beyond 2026-27 and is being reviewed mid-budget cycle.
findings.detail: The MTFP approved in February set out a balanced position but noted 'limited headroom beyond 2026/27', which was contingent on successful delivery of savings and containment of cost and demand pressures. The MTFP is now under review and will continue into autumn as part of the budget-setting process, suggesting the initial assumptions are being reassessed.
findings.matters: Limited MTFP headroom combined with demonstrated inability to manage £7.4m demand-led overspends in 2025-26 signals material medium-term budget stress. The need for savings to achieve balance rather than existing headroom indicates structural budget challenges.
findings.figures: Limited headroom beyond 2026-27; £7.442m service overspends in 2025-26; General Reserve of £24.2m (2.8% of budget requirement)
findings.quote: The MTFP, approved by Full Council in February, set out a balanced position with limited headroom beyond 2026/27, which was contingent on the successful delivery of savings and the containment of cost and demand pressures within budget assumptions at that time.
